		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We are a bank holding company and our operations are conducted by </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">direct and indirect subsidiaries, each of which is a separate and distinct legal entity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Substantially all of our assets are held by </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">such</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> subsidiaries</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">; and our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ability to pay dividends depends on our receipt of dividends from our direct and indirect subsidiaries.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank is our primary source of dividends.&nbsp;&nbsp;Dividend payments from Royal Bank are subject to legal and regulatory limitations, generally based on net profits and retained earnings, imposed by the various banking regulatory agencies. The ability of Royal Bank to pay dividends is also subject to its profitability, financial condition, capital expenditures and other cash flow requirements. At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, as a result of significant losses within Royal Bank from prior years, we had an accumulated deficit and therefore would not have been able to declare and pay any cash dividends.&nbsp;&nbsp;There is no assurance that our subsidiaries will be able to pay dividends in the future</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> or that we will generate adequate cash flow to pay dividends in the future. </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We suspended regular quarterly cash dividends on the Series A Preferred Stock in August 2009 and, accordingly, are not permitted at this time to pay dividends on our Class A or Class B Common Stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, under the terms of the informal agreement with the Federal Reserve Bank, we are prohibited from redeemi</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ng the Series A Preferred Stock</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> or paying any dividends on shares of our stock without the prior written approval of the Reserve Bank and the Director of the Division of Banking Supervision and Regulation of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.&nbsp;&nbsp;Failure to pay dividends on our stock could have a material adverse effect on the market price of our Class A Common Stock.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Our ability to use net operating loss carryforwards to reduce future tax payments may be limited.</font>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">T</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">he ability to use NOLs will be dependent on our ability to generate taxable income. The NOLs may expire before we generate sufficient taxable income. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">There </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">was </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">a &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$4.0 million</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> NOL</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> carryover</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> from the acquisition of Knoblauch State Bank</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> that expired in 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">There were no NOLs that expired </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">in 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Refer to &#x201C;Accounting for Income Tax Expense&#x201D; in</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Item 7, &#x201C;Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#x201D;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> of this Report.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">We may not be able to fully recover o</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">ur deferred tax asset </font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">valuation allowance</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We recognize deferred tax assets </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">(&#x201C;DTA&#x201D;) </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and liabilities based on differences between the financial statement carrying amounts and the tax bases of assets and liabilities. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We are required to establish a valuation allowance for DTAs and record a charge to income or shareholders' equity if management determines, based on available evidence at the time the determination is made, that it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management evaluates the DTAs for recoverability using a consistent approach which considers the relative impact of negative and positive evidence, including historical profitability and projections of future reversals of temporary differences and future taxable income. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">These determinations are inherently subjective and dependent upon estimates and judgments concerning management&#x2019;s evaluation of both positive and negative evidence.</font>
		</p>

&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;">As a result of this conclusion</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, we released $5.4 million of our valuation allowance previously recorded on the net DTAs and credited income tax expense</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The ability to recognize the remaining deferred tax assets that continue to be subject to a valuation allowance will be evaluated on a quarterly basis to determine if there are any significant events that would affect the ability to utilize these deferred tax assets. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The release of the remaining</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> valuation allowance would have a positive impact on future earnings.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">There can be no assurance, however, as to when we could be in a position to recapture the remaining DTA valuation allowance. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The deferred tax assets/(liabilities), net of valuation allowances, totaled $5.7 million and $(308) thousand at December 31, 2015 and 2014, respectively.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">T</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">he deferred tax asset valuation allowance was $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">30</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and $39.1 million </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015 and 2014, respectively</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Refer to &#x201C;Accounting for Income Tax Expense&#x201D; in</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Item 7, &#x201C;Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#x201D;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> of this Report.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Competition from other financial institutions may adversely affect our profitability.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We face substantial competition in originating commercial and consumer loans. This competition comes principally from other banks, savings institutions, mortgage banking companies and other lenders.&nbsp;&nbsp;Many of our competitors enjoy advantages, including greater financial resources and higher lending limits, a wider geographic presence, more accessible branch office locations, the ability to offer a wider array of services or more favorable pricing alternatives, as well as lower origination and operating costs. This competition could reduce our net income by decreasing the number and size of loans that we originate and the interest rates we may charge on these loans. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In attracting business and consumer deposits, Royal Bank faces substantial competition from other insured depository institutions such as banks, savings institutions and credit unions, as well as institutions offering uninsured investment alternatives, including money market funds.&nbsp;&nbsp;Many of our competitors enjoy advantages, including greater financial resources, more aggressive marketing campaigns, better brand recognition and more branch locations.&nbsp;&nbsp;These competitors may offer higher interest rates than we do, which could decrease the deposits that we attract or require us to increase our rates to retain existing deposits or attract new deposits.&nbsp;&nbsp;Increased deposit competition could adversely affect our ability to generate the funds necessary for lending operations. As a result, we may need to seek other sources of funds that may be more expensive to obtain and could increase our cost of funds. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> banking and non-banking subsidiaries also compete with non-bank providers of financial services, such as brokerage firms, consumer finance companies, credit unions, insurance agencies, peer to peer lenders and governmental organizations which may offer more favorable terms.&nbsp;&nbsp;Some of our non-bank competitors are not subject to the same extensive regulations that govern our banking operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;As a result, such non-bank competitors may have advantages over </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> banking and non-banking subsidiaries in providing certain products and services.&nbsp;&nbsp;This competition may reduce or limit our margins on banking and non-banking services, reduce our market share, and adversely affect our earnings and financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Our ability to manage liquidity is always critical in our operation, but more so today given the uncertainty within the capital markets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We monitor and manage our liquidity position on a regular basis to insure that adequate funds are in place to manage the day to day operations and to cover routine fluctuations in available funds. However, our funding decisions can be influenced by unplanned events. These unplanned events include, but are not limited to, the inability to fund asset growth, difficulty renewing or replacing funds that mature, the ability to maintain or draw down lines of credit with other financial institutions, significant customer withdrawals of deposits, and market disruptions. We have a liquidity contingency plan in the event liquidity falls below an acceptable level, however in today&#x2019;s economic environment, we are not certain that those sources of liquid funds will be available in the future when required. As a result, loan growth may be curtailed to maintain adequate liquidity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, loans may need to be sold in the secondary market, investments may need to be sold or deposits may need to be raised at above market interest rates to maintain liquidity.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Negative publicity could damage our reputation and adversely impact our business and financial results. </font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Reputation risk, or the risk to our earnings and capital from negative publicity, is inherent in our business.&nbsp;&nbsp;Negative publicity can result from our actual or alleged conduct in any number of activities, including lending practices, corporate governance, acquisitions, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">cyber-attacks, breach in security, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and actions taken by government regulators and community organizations in response to those activities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Negative publicity can adversely affect our ability to keep and attract customers and can expose us to litigation and regulatory action.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although we take steps to minimize reputation risk in dealing with customers and other </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">Our business is subject to interest rate risk</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;"> and variations in interest rates may negatively affect our financial performance.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Changes in the interest rate environment may reduce profits. The primary source of our income is the differential or &#x201C;spread&#x201D; between the interest earned on loans, securities and other interest-earning assets, and interest paid on deposits, borrowings and other interest-bearing liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;As prevailing interest rates change, net interest spreads are affected by the difference between the maturities and re-pricing characteristics of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, loan volume and yields are affected by market interest rates on loans, and rising interest rates generally are associated with a lower volume of loan originations.&nbsp;&nbsp;An increase in the general level of interest rates may also adversely affect the ability of certain borrowers to pay the interest on and principal of their obligations.&nbsp;&nbsp;Accordingly, changes in levels of market interest rates could materially adversely affect our net interest spread, asset quality, loan origination volume, pre-payment speeds and overall profitability. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In 2015, t</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">he</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> branch </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">located in the sold building </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">was</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> relocated to a leased facility within the same market area of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">that</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> location.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; 		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">ITEM 3.&nbsp;&nbsp;LEGAL PROCEEDINGS</font><a name="ITEM3LEGALPROCEEDINGS_548395"></a>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">P</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">rior to December 31, 2013,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Royal Bank held a 60% equity interest in each of CSC and RTL.&nbsp;&nbsp;CSC and RTL acquired, through public</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> auction, delinquent tax liens in various jurisdictions thereby assuming a superior lien position to most other lien holders, including mortgage lien holders.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2012, the former President of CSC and RTL, CSC, RTL and the Company were named defendants, among others, in a Consolidated Master Class Action Complaint (the &#x201C;Complaint&#x201D;) filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey (&#x201C;Court&#x201D;) on behalf of a proposed class of taxpayers who became delinquent in paying their municipal tax obligations</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Complaint</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> alleged a conspiracy to rig bids in municipal tax lien auctions.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">During 2013, the Company, Royal Bank, CSC, and RTL reached a settlement agreement with plaintiffs to settle the litigation for $1.65 million and other terms and conditions, including an opportunity for members of the proposed settlement class whose tax liens are currently held by CSC or RTL to redeem those liens for a one-time cash payment equaling 85% of the redemption amount by making such payment within 35 days of the date of written notice.&nbsp;&nbsp;The proposed settlement class does not include, and therefore the offer to redeem does not apply to, tax liens acquired at 0% interest or at a premium.&nbsp;&nbsp;The settlement is subject to Court approval after notice and a hearing.&nbsp;&nbsp;Members of the proposed settlement class will have an opportunity to object to the proposed settlement or opt-out.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Dividends</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Subject to certain limitations imposed by law or </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> articles of incorporation, the Board of Directors of the Company may declare a dividend on shares of Class A or Class B Common Stock.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> did not pay cash dividends on </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">common stock in </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Future dividends depend upon net income, capital requirements, and appropriate legal restrictions and other factors relevant at the time the Board of Directors of the Company considers dividend policy.&nbsp;&nbsp;Cash necessary to fund dividends available for dividend distributions to the shareholders of the Company must initially come primarily from dividends paid by its direct and indirect subsidiaries, including Royal Bank</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to the Company.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Under the Pennsylvania Business Corporation Law, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> may pay dividends only if, after giving effect to the dividend payment, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">total assets would exceed </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> total liabilities plus the amount necessary to satisfy preferential rights of holders of senior shareholders, and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we are</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> solvent and would not be rendered insolvent by the dividend payment. There are also restrictions set forth in the Pennsylvania Banking Code of 1965 (the &#x201C;Code&#x201D;), and in the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (&#x201C;FDIC Act&#x201D;) concerning the payment of dividends by Royal Bank.&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the Code, no dividends may be paid except from &#x201C;accumulated net earnings&#x201D; (generally retained earnings).&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the FDIC Act, no dividend may be paid if a bank is in arrears in the payment of any insurance assessment due to the FDIC.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, dividends paid by Royal Bank to the Company would be prohibited if the effect thereof would cause Royal Bank&#x2019;s capital to be reduced below applicable minimum capital requirements.&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, the restrictions on Royal Bank&#x2019;s dividend payments are directly applicable to the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;See &#x201C;Note 1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &#x2013; Shareholder&#x2019;s Equity&#x201D; of the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements in Item 8 of this Report.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> board of directors took this action in consultation with the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia as required by regulatory policy guidance.&nbsp;&nbsp;As of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Series A Preferred stock dividend in </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">arrears </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">including interest </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">was $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">8.9</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million and has not been recognized in the consolidated financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;In the event </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> declared the preferred dividend</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">capital ratios would be negatively affected</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> however, they would remain above the required minimum ratios.&nbsp;&nbsp;In February 2014, the preferred cumulative dividend rate prospectively increased from 5% to 9% per annum.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Critical Accounting Policies, Judgments and Estimates </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In preparing the consolidated financial statements in accordance with United States generally accepted accounting principles (&#x201C;U.S. GAAP&#x201D;), management is required to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in the consolidated financial statements and the accompanying notes. These estimates and assumptions are based on information available as of the date of the consolidated financial statements; therefore, actual results could differ from those estimates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The accounting and reporting policies of the Company conform to accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America and general practices within the financial services industry.&nbsp;&nbsp;Critical accounting policies, judgments and estimates relate to </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">other-than-temporary impairment losses on investment securities, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">allowance for loan and lease losses, the valuation of other real estate owned (&#x201C;OREO&#x201D;), the valuation of deferred tax assets, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">fair value measurements, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">net periodic pension costs and the pension benefit obligation. The policies which significantly affect the determination of the Company&#x2019;s financial position, results of operations and cash flows are summarized in &#x201C;Note 1 - Summary of Significant Accounting Polices&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements and are discussed in the section captioned &#x201C;Recent Accounting Pronouncements&#x201D; of Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations, included in Items 7 and 8 of this Report, each of which is incorporated herein by reference.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Investment Securities</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We evaluate</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> securities for other-than-temporary impairment (&#x201C;OTTI&#x201D;) at least on a quarterly basis.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We assess</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> whether OTTI is present when the fair value of a security is less than its amortized cost.&nbsp;&nbsp;All investment securities are evaluated for OTTI </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">25</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">under FASB ASC Topic 320, &#x201C;Investments-Debt &amp; Equity Securities&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 320&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;Under ASC Topic 320, OTTI is considered to have occurred with respect to debt securities (1) if an entity intends to sell the security; (2) if it is more likely than not an entity will be required to sell the security before recovery of its amortized cost basis; or (3) the present value of the expected cash flows is not sufficient to recover the entire amortized cost basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the amount of the OTTI recognized in earnings depends on whether an entity intends to sell or will more likely than not be required to sell the security.&nbsp;&nbsp;If an entity intends to sell the security or will be required to sell the security, the OTTI shall be recognized in earnings equal to the entire difference between the fair value and the amortized cost basis at the balance sheet date.&nbsp;&nbsp;If an entity does not intend to sell the security and it is not more likely than not that the entity will be required to sell the security before the recovery of its amortized cost basis, the OTTI shall be separated into two amounts, the credit-related loss and the noncredit-related loss. The credit-related loss is based on the present value of the expected cash flows and is recognized in earnings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The allowance for loan and lease losses (the &#x201C;allowance&#x201D;) represents management&#x2019;s estimate of losses inherent in the loan</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> and lease</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> portfolio as of the statement of financial condition date and is recorded as a reduction to loans and leases. The allowance is increased by the provision for loan and lease losses, and decreased by charge-offs, net of recoveries. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> consider that the determination of the allowance involves a higher degree of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">judgment and complexity than our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> other significant accounting policies.&nbsp;&nbsp;The allowance is calculated with the objective of maintaining a reserve level believed by management to be sufficient to absorb estimated credit losses.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The allowance is based on </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> past loan loss experience, known and inherent risks in the portfolio, adverse situations that may affect the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay, the estimated value of any underlying collateral, the composition of the loan portfolio, current economic conditions and other relevant factors. This evaluation is inherently subjective as it requires material estimates that may be susceptible to significant revision as more information becomes available. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">All of these factors may be susceptible to significant change.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">While management uses the best information available to make loan loss allowance evaluations, adjustments to the allowance may be necessary based on changes in economic and other conditions or changes in accounting guidance. In addition, the FDIC, as an integral part of its examination processes, periodically reviews our allowance for loan </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">and lease losses. The FDI</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">C may require the recognition of adjustments to the allowance for loan losses based on their judgment of information available to them at the time of their examinations. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">To the extent actual outcomes differ from management estimates, additional provisions for loan and lease losses may be required that would adversely impact earnings in future periods. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We also have a</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> reserve for unfunded lending commitments</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">, which</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> represents management&#x2019;s estimate of losses inherent in </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">those</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> commitments</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;The reserve for unfunded loan commitments is adjusted by a provision for credit losses on off-balance sheet credit exposures</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> and is recorded in other liabilities on the consolidated statement of financial condition. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">See &#x201C;Note 1 - Summary of Significant Accounting Policies&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements included in Item 8 of this report. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Other Real Estate Owned</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Assets acquired through, or in lieu of, loan foreclosure are held for sale and are initially recorded at fair value less costs to sell at the date of foreclosure, establishing a new cost basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Foreclosed real estate properties acquired through the tax certificate portfolio are transferred at the lower of cost or fair value principally due to uncertainty around the fair value of the foreclosed properties.&nbsp;&nbsp;Subsequent to foreclosure, valuations are periodically performed by management and the assets are carried at the lower of carrying amount recorded at acquisition date or fair value less costs to sell.&nbsp;&nbsp;Third-party appraisals or agreements of sale are utilized to determine fair value of the loan collateral while BPOs, agreements of sale, or in some cases, third-party appraisals are utilized to value properties from the tax certificate portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;Revenue and expenses from operations and changes in the valuation allowance are included in other expenses.&nbsp;&nbsp;For fair value measurement, OREO is included in level 3 assets. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Deferred Tax Assets</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We recognize</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> deferred tax assets and liabilities for the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">future tax consequences related to differences between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and liabilities and their respective tax bases</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Deferred tax assets are subject to management&#x2019;s judgment based upon available evidence that future realization is more likely than not.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Times;font-size:10pt;">We are</font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Times;font-size:10pt;"> required to establish a valuation allowance for deferred tax assets and record a charge to income or shareholders' equity if management determines, based on </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Times;font-size:10pt;">all </font><font style="display:inline;font-family:Times;font-size:10pt;">available evidence at the time the determination is made, that it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">These estimates and judgments are inherently subjective. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Management evaluates the DTAs for recoverability using a consistent approach which considers the relative impact of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">26</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">negative and positive evidence, including historical profitability and projections of future reversals of temporary differences and future taxable income. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">In evaluating our ability to recover deferred tax assets, management considers all available positive and negative evidence, including our past operating results and our forecast of future taxable income. In determining future taxable income, assumptions are made for the amount of taxable income, the reversal of temporary differences and </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">potentially </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">the implementation of feasible and prudent tax planning strategies. These assumptions are consistent with the plans and estimates management uses to manage </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> business. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Based on the analysis of the DTAs at December 31, 2015, </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;">management concluded that it is more likely than not that a portion of the net DTA will be realized by the Company in the future.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;As a result of this conclusion, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we released $5.4 million of our valuation allowance previously recorded on the net DTAs and credited income tax expense, which was partially offset by the current income expense for the year. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The ability to recognize the remaining deferred tax assets that continue to be subject to a valuation allowance will be evaluated on a quarterly basis to determine if there are any significant events that would affect the ability to utilize these deferred tax assets. There can be no assurance, however, as to when we could be in a position to recapture the remaining DTA valuation allowance. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">, the DTA valuation allowance was $</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">30.6</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> million compared to $</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">39.1</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;For more information r</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">efer to &#x201C;Note 12</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">-</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Income Taxes&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements in</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Item 8 of this Report.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Fair Value Measurements</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> use fair value measurements to record fair value adjustments to certain assets to determine fair value disclosures. Investment and mortgage-backed securities available for sale are recorded at fair value on a recurring basis. Additionally, from time to time, </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> may be required to record at fair value other assets on a nonrecurring basis, such as impaired loans, real estate owned and certain other assets. These nonrecurring fair value adjustments typically involve application of lower-of-cost-or-market accounting or write-downs of individual assets. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">FASB ASC Topic 820 &#x201C;Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 820&#x201D;), </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">establishes a fair value hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs to valuation methods</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> used to measure fair value.&nbsp; The three levels of the fair value hierarchy under ASC Topic 820 are as follows:</font>
		</p>

				</td>

						<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Level 2:</font></p>

Valuation techniques include matrix pricing </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">which is a mathematical technique used widely in the industry to value debt securities without relying exclusively on quoted market prices for the specific securities but rather by relying on the securities&#x2019; relationship to other benchmark quoted prices.</font></p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Under ASC Topic 820, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> base </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> fair values on the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">It is our policy to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs when developing fair value measurements, in accordance with the fair value hierarchy in FASB ASC Topic 820. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Fair value measurements for assets where there exists limited or no observable market data and, therefore, are based primarily upon </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> or other third-party&#x2019;s estimates, are often calculated based on the characteristics of the asset, the economic and competitive environment and other such factors. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Management uses its best judgment in estimating the fair value of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> financial instruments; however,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> there are inherent weaknesses in any estimation technique.&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, for substantially all financial instruments, the fair value estimates herein are not necessarily indicative of the amounts </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> could have realized in a sales transaction on the dates indicated.&nbsp;&nbsp;The estimated fair value amounts have been measured as of their respective period end and have not been re-evaluated or updated for purposes of these financial statements subsequent to those respective dates.&nbsp;&nbsp;As such, the estimated fair values of these financial instruments</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> subsequent to the respective reporting dates may be different than the amounts reported at each period-end.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Additionally,</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> changes in the underlying assumptions used, including discount rates and estimates of future cash flows, could significantly affect the results of current or future valuations.</font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Benefit Plans</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We have</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a noncontributory nonqualified defined benefit pension plan (&#x201C;Pension Plan&#x201D;) covering certain eligible employees.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Pension Plan provides retirement benefits under pension trust agreements.&nbsp;&nbsp;The benefits are based on years of service and the employee&#x2019;s compensation during the highest three consecutive years during the last 10&nbsp;years of employment.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> account for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> pension</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> plan</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 715 &#x201C;Compensation-Retirement Benefits&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 715&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;ASC Topic 715 requires the recognition of a plan&#x2019;s over-funded or under-funded status as an asset or liability with an offsetting adjustment to AOCI.&nbsp;&nbsp;ASC Topic 715 requires the determination of the fair values of plans assets at a company&#x2019;s year-end and recognition of actuarial gains and losses, prior service costs or credits, and transition assets or obligations as a component of AOCI.&nbsp;&nbsp;These amounts will be subsequently recognized as components of net periodic benefits cost.&nbsp;&nbsp;Further, actuarial gains and losses that arise in subsequent periods that are not initially recognized as a component of net periodic benefit cost will be recognized as a component of AOCI.&nbsp;&nbsp;Those amounts will subsequently be recognized as a component of net periodic benefit cost as they are amortized during future periods.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Net pension expense consists of service costs and interest costs.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We accrue</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> pension costs as incurred.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Benefit payments are expected to be </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">substantially </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">made from insurance policies owned by the Company.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a capital accumulation and salary reduction plan under Section 401(k) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended.&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the plan, all employees are eligible to contribute up to the maximum allowed by Internal Revenue Service (&#x201C;IRS&#x201D;) regulation, with the Company matching 100% of any contribution between 1% and 5% subject to a $2,500 per employee annual limit.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The 401(k) matching contribution was $134 thousand and $148 thousand for&nbsp;&nbsp;2015 and 2014, respectively</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Recent Accounting Pronouncements</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Results of Operations</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Financial Highlights and Business Results</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> results of operations depend primarily on net interest income.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Its level is a function of the average balance of interest-earning assets, the average balance of interest-bearing liabilities, and the spread between the yield on assets and liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;In turn, these factors are influenced by the pricing and mix of our interest-earning assets and funding sources.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, net interest income is affected by market and economic conditions, which influence rates on loan and deposit growth.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Interest-earning assets consist principally of loans and investment securities, while interest-bearing liabilities consist primarily of deposits and borrowings.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Refer to the &#x201C;Net Interest Income and Net Interest Margin&#x201D; section below for additional information on interest yield and cost. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;Net income is also affected by the provision for loan and lease losses and the level of non-interest income as well as by non-interest expenses, including salary and employee benefits, occupancy expenses and other operating expenses.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The financial results for 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> illustrate </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">further</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> progress </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">on&nbsp;our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">goal of consistent profitability and serving</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our four key constituents:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;customers, shareholders, co-workers, and community.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our financial performance continues to allow us to expand the Royal Bank brand through our relationship based </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">customer</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> model.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Loan</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> growth in commercial, consumer, and leasing segments and more economical delivery channels, including a loan production office, are helping drive customer growth.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We continue our focus on modernizing the ways customers can access our products and services.&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2015, we introduced a new custom branded &#x201C;smart phone&#x201D; application, which provides a simpler online banking experience and online loan applications are increasing.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">These results and continued progress come at a time when competition, low interest rates, regulatory requirements and domestic and global markets greatly challenge the banking industry.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our ability to generate consistent earnings led to the partial reversal of the valuation allowance on the deferred tax assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;For further discussion on the deferred tax assets see &#x201C;Accounting for Income Taxes.&#x201D;&nbsp; </font>

</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Prior to 2015, a full valuation allowance was recorded against the DTA based on the available evidence at that time.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management performs this analysis on an annual basis or sooner if significant events occur which would affect the ability to utilize these DTAs in the future.&nbsp; 		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We assess</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> whether OTTI is present when the fair value of a security is less than its amortized cost.&nbsp;&nbsp;All investment securities are evaluated for OTTI under FASB ASC Topic 320, &#x201C;Investments-Debt &amp; Equity Securities&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 320&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;Non-agency collateralized mortgage obligations may be evaluated under FASB ASC Topic 320 Subtopic 40, &#x201C;Beneficial Interests in Securitized Financial Assets&#x201D; under FASB ASC Topic 325, &#x201C;Investments-Other&#x201D;.&nbsp;&nbsp;In determining whether OTTI exists, management considers numerous factors, including but not limited to: (1) the length of time and the extent to which the fair value is less than the amortized cost, (2) </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> intent to hold or sell the security, (3) the financial condition and results of the issuer including changes in capital, (4) the credit rating of the issuer, (5) analysts&#x2019; earnings estimate, (6) industry trends specific to the security, and (7) timing of debt maturity and status of debt payments.&nbsp;&nbsp;If </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we intend</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to sell a security or will be required to sell a security, the OTTI is recognized in earnings equal to the entire difference between the fair value and the amortized cost basis at the balance sheet date.&nbsp;&nbsp;If </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;d</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">o</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> not intend to sell a security and it is not more likely than not that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> will be required to sell a security before the recovery of its amortized cost basis, the OTTI is separated into two amounts, the credit related loss and the loss related to other factors.&nbsp;&nbsp;The credit related loss is based on the present value of the expected cash flows and is recognized in earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;The noncredit-related loss is based on other factors such as illiquidity and is recognized in other comprehensive inc</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ome.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> recorded </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">an OTTI charge of $14 thousand related to a private equity investment in 2015 compared to $41 thousand in 2014.</font>
		</p>
