		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> primary earning assets are loans, representing approximately </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">64.8</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">% of average interest-earning assets during </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We originate loans primarily in the greater Philadelphia metropolitan area as well as selected locations throughout the Mid-Atlantic region. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> also ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> participated with other financial institutions in selected construction and land development loans outside these geographic areas.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The loan portfolio consists primarily of commercial demand loans and commercial mortgages secured by real estate, leases, and to a significantly lesser extent, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">tax liens and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">residential loans comprised of one to four family residential and home equity loans.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We have a concentration of credit risk in commercial real estate and construction and land development loans, which represented 54.8% of total loans at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> compared to 53.2% of total loans at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">During </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, total loans grew $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">84.0</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million from $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">415.1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">499.1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;The growth was attributed to new loan originations partially offset by balances being paid down, payoffs, charge-offs, and transfers to OREO.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The loans receivable portfolio is segmented into commercial loans, construction and development loans, residential loans, leases, tax certificates, and consumer loans. The commercial loan segment consists of the following classes: commercial real estate loans, multi-family real estate loans, and other commercial loans, which are also generally known as commercial and industrial loans or commercial business loans. The construction and development loan segment consists of the following classes: residential construction and commercial construction loans. Residential construction loans are made for the acquisition of and/or construction on a lot or lots on which a residential dwelling is to be built. Commercial construction loans are made for the purpose of acquiring, developing and/or constructing a commercial structure. The residential loan segment consists of the following classes: one- to four-family first lien residential mortgage loans, home equity lines of credit, and home equity loans.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We classify</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> leases as finance leases, in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 840, &#x201C;Leases&#x201D;. The difference between </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> gross investment in the lease and the cost or carrying amount of the leased property, if different, is recorded as unearned income, which is amortized to income over the lease term by the interest method.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificate segment includes </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">delinquent property tax certificates that have been acquired through public auctions in various jurisdictions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificates assume a lien position that is generally superior to any mortgage liens that are on the property and have certain foreclosure rights as defined by state law.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificates are predominantly in New Jersey. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ceased acquiring new tax certificates in 2010.&nbsp;&nbsp;Consumer loans includes cash secured and unsecured loans and </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">lines of credit. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Commercial Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> The commercial real estate loan portfolio consists primarily of loans secured by office buildings, retail and industrial use buildings, strip shopping centers, mixed-use and other properties used for commercial purposes primarily located in our market area. Although terms for commercial real estate and multi-family loans vary, the underwriting standards generally allow for terms up to 10 years with the interest rate being reset in the sixth year and with monthly amortization not greater than 25 years and loan-to-value ratios of not more than 80%. Interest rates are either fixed or adjustable and are </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">predominantly </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">based upon the prime rate or a borrowing rate from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Pittsburgh plus a margin. Prepayment fees are charged on most loans in the event of early repayment. Generally, the personal guarantees of the principals are obtained as additional collateral for commercial real estate and multi-family real estate loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Commercial and multi-family real estate loans generally present a higher level of risk than loans secured by one- to four-family residences. This greater risk is due to several factors, including the concentration of principal in a limited number of loans and borrowers, the effect of general economic conditions on income producing properties and the increased difficulty of evaluating and monitoring these types of loans. Furthermore, the repayment of loans secured by commercial and multi-family real estate is typically dependent upon the successful operation of the related real estate project. If the cash flow from the project is reduced (for example, if leases are not obtained or renewed, a bankruptcy court modifies a lease term, or a major tenant is unable to fulfill its lease obligations), the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay the loan may be impaired.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Our commercial business loans generally have been made to small to mid-sized businesses predominantly located in our market area. The commercial business loans are either a revolving line of credit or for a fixed term of generally 10 years or less. Interest rates are adjustable, indexed to a published prime rate of interest, or fixed. Generally, equipment, machinery, real property or other corporate assets secure such loans. Personal guarantees from the business principals are generally obtained as additional collateral. Generally, commercial business loans are characterized as having higher risks associated with them than single-family residential loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">38</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> underwriting procedures include evaluations of the stability of the property&#x2019;s cash flow history, future operating projections, current and projected occupancy levels, location and physical condition. Generally, </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">we require</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> a debt service ratio (the ratio of net cash flows from operations before the payment of debt service to debt service) of not less than 120%. We also evaluate the credit and financial condition of the borrower, and if applicable, the guarantor. Appraisal reports prepared by independent appraisers are obtained on each loan to substantiate the property&#x2019;s market value, and are reviewed prior to the closing of the loan.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Construction and Development Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">originate</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> construction loans to builders and developers predominantly in our market area. Construction and development loans are riskier than other loan types because they are more speculative in nature. Deteriorating economic or environmental conditions can negatively affect a project. Construction loans are also more difficult to evaluate and monitor.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to mitigate some of the risks inherent in construction lending, limits are placed on the number of units that can be built on a speculative basis based upon the reputation and financial position of the builder, his/her present obligations, the location of the property and prior sales in the development and the surrounding area. Additionally, the construction budget is reviewed prior to loan origination and the properties under construction are inspected. During the construction phase of a real estate project, the loan requires interest payments only.&nbsp;&nbsp;Construction loans generally are for 12 to 18 months with loan-to-value ratios of not more than 75%.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;Most construction loans are assigned an initial risk rating of pass-watch due to the riskier nature of the loan.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Residential Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> residential mortgages were acquired in recent years in pool purchases and are secured primarily by properties located in </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> primary market and surrounding areas.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">originate home equity loans and home equity lines of credit in our market area with a </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">general </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">maximum amount of $250</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> thousand.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> The collateral must be the borrower&#x2019;s primary residence and the loan-to-value does not exceed 80%. Home equity lines of credit are variable rate and are indexed to the prime rate.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our home equity loans are either first or second liens and have a fixed rate.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Consumer Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> originate cash-secured and unsecured loans and lines of credit to individuals.&nbsp;&nbsp;Unsecured loans and lines of credit have a maximum amount of $15</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> thousand</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Unsecured consumer loans generally have a higher interest rate than residential loans because they have additional credit risk associated with them.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In the past w</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">e</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> made loans to the officers and directors of the Company and to their associates.&nbsp;&nbsp;In accordance with Regulation O related party loans are made on substantially the same terms, including interest rates and collateral, as those prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with unrelated persons and do not involve more than normal risk of collectability.&nbsp;&nbsp;The</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">re were no relate</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">d</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> party loans outstanding</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Total payments received on related party loans in 2014 were $100</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> thousand</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Credit Classification Process</font><font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;"> and Credit Risk Management</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We use</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a nine point grading risk classification system commonly used in the financial services industry.&nbsp;&nbsp;The first four classifications are rated Pass.&nbsp;&nbsp;The riskier classifications include Pass-Watch, Special Mention, Substandard, Doubtful and Loss.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">During the underwriting process, the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Chief Credit Officer (&#x201C;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">CCO</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> assigns each loan with an initial risk rating, which is approved by the appropriate loan committee. From time to time, and at the general direction of any of the various loan committees, the ratings may be changed based on the findings of that committee. Items considered in assigning ratings include the financial strength of the borrower and/or guarantors, the type of collateral, the collateral lien position, the type of loan and loan structure, any potential risk inherent in the specific loan type, higher than normal monitoring of the loan or any other factor deemed appropriate by any of the various committees for changing the rating of the loan. Any such change in rating is reflected in the minutes of that committee. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The loan review function is outsourced to a third party vendor which examines credit quality and portfolio management. The loan review vendor applies </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> loan rating system to specific credits and reviews approximately 50% of the total commercial loan portfolio. Emphasis is on the larger new and seasoned loan relationships and includes criticized and classified loans. Additionally, the loan review vendor ensures that all critical industry segments are adequately represented in their review. The loan review vendor will also review loans specifically requested by management. Upon completion of a loan review, a copy of any review receiving an adverse classification by the reviewer is presented to the Classified, Charge-off and Impairment Committee (&#x201C;CCIC&#x201D;) for discussion. The CCO is the primary bank officer dealing with the third party vendor during the reviews. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Loans on </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Special Assets Committee list are also subject to loan review even though they are receiving the daily attention of an assigned </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">individual</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">the</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> attention of the Special Assets Committee.&nbsp;&nbsp;A watch list is maintained and reviewed at each meeting of CCIC. CCIC was formed to formalize the process and documentation required to classify, remove from classification, impair or charge-off a loan. The CCIC, which is comprised of the CEO, CFO, CCO, C</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">hief Lending Officer </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">40</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">(&#x201C;C</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">LO</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, and Chief Accounting Officer (&#x201C;CAO&#x201D;) meet as required and provide regular updated reports to the Board of Directors.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans are added to the watch list, even though the loans may be current or less than 30 days delinquent if they exhibit elements of substandard creditworthiness. The watch list contains a statement for each loan as to why it merits special attention, and this list is distributed to the Board of Directors on a </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">quarter</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ly basis. Loans may be removed from the watch list if the CCIC determines that exception items have been resolved or creditworthiness has improved. Additionally, if loans become serious collection matters and are listed on </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> monthly delinquent loan or Special Assets Committee lists, they may be removed from the watch list.&nbsp;&nbsp;Minutes outlining the CCIC&#x2019;s findings and recommendations are issued after each meeting for follow-up by individual loan officers.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Total non-accrual </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">loans </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> were $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5.5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million compared to $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">9.8</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;The $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4.3 million</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> decline in non-accrual </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">loans was the result of a $4.1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million reduction in existing non-accrual loan balances through payments or payoffs, $2.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million in charge-offs related to impairment, and transfers to OREO of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4.3</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million, which collectively were offset by $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">6.6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million in additions. The majority of the new non-accrual activity and transfers to OREO originated from the tax certificate portfolio.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Commercial real estate, tax certificates, and leases represented 27.2%, 20.5%, and 19.8%, respectively, of the total $5.5 million in non-accrual loans at December 31, 2015.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Impaired Loans</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We identify</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a loan as impaired when it is probable that interest and principal will not be collected according to the contractual terms of the loan agreement.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">For all classes of loans receivable, with the exception of tax certificates, the accrual of interest is discontinued on a loan when management believes that the borrower&#x2019;s financial condition is such that collection of principal and interest is doubtful or when a loan becomes 90 days past due. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Impaired loans include TDRs. Excess proceeds received over the principal amounts due on impaired non-accrual loans are recognized as income on a cash basis. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">41</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">recognize income under the accrual basis when the principal payments on the loans become current and the collateral on the loan is sufficient to cover the outstanding obligation to the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;If </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">these factors do not exist, we do</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> not recognize interest income. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">If interest had accrued on these loans, such income would have been approximately $703 thousand and $1.0 million for the years</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ended </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, respectively. At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Company had </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">no</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> loans past due 90 days or more on which interest continues to </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">accrue.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Total</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> cash collected on impai</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">red loans during the year ended</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> was </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$9.6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$7.0</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">million respectively, of which </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$8.4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$6.4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million was credited to the principal balance outstanding on such loans, respectively.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">*</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Includes loans held for sale during 2014.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Troubled Debt Restructurings</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">A loan modification is deemed a TDR when two conditions are met: 1) the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty and 2) concessions are made by the Company that would not otherwise be considered for a borrower or collateral with similar credit risk characteristics.&nbsp;&nbsp;All loans classified as TDRs are considered to be impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;TDRs are returned to an accrual status when the loan is brought current, has performed in accordance with the contractual restructured terms for a reasonable period of time (generally six months) and the ultimate collectibility of the total contractual restructured principal and interest is no longer in doubt.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Company had </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">six</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> TDRs, with a total carrying value of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2.6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million. At the time of the modifications, three of the loans were already classified as impaired non-accrual loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Company had </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">12</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> TDRs with a total carrying value of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">8.8</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The $6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.2 million decline in TDRs was mainly due to principal payments and payoffs.&nbsp;&nbsp;One construction and land development TDR was transferred to OREO in 2015.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> policy for TDRs is to recognize income on currently performing restructured loans under the accrual method.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The following table details the Company&#x2019;s TDRs that are on an accrual status and a non-accrual status at December 31, 2015.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">42</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We may obtain physical possession of real estate collateralizing residential mortgage loans or home equity loans through or in lieu of, foreclosure. As of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, we </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">did not have any</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> foreclosed residential real estate property as a result of physical possession. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">However</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, as of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, we had residential mortgage loans with a carrying value of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$399 thousand</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> collateralized by residential real estate property for which formal foreclosure proceedings were in process.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 1pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:1pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Potential Problem Loans </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Potential problem loans are loans not currently classified as non-performing loans, but for which management has doubts as to the borrowers&#x2019; ability to comply with present repayment terms. The loans are usually delinquent more than 30 days but less than 90 days. Potential problem loans amounted to approximately $3.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">3</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million and $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">3.4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, respectively. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Allowance for loan and lease losses (&#x201C;allowance&#x201D;)</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> loan and lease portfolio (the &#x201C;credit portfolio&#x201D;) is subject to varying degrees of credit risk. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We maintain</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> an allowance to absorb losses in the loan and lease portfolio. The allowance is based on the review and evaluation of the loan and lease portfolio, along with ongoing, quarterly assessments of the probable losses inherent in that portfolio. The allowance represents an estimation made pursuant to FASB ASC Topic 450, &#x201C;Contingencies&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 450&#x201D;) or FASB ASC Topic 310, &#x201C;Receivables&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 310&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;The adequacy of the allowance is determined through evaluation of the credit portfolio, and involves consideration of a number of factors, as outlined below, to establish a prudent level.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Determination of the allowance is inherently subjective and requires significant estimates, including estimated losses on pools of homogeneous loans and leases based on historical loss experience and consideration of current economic trends, which may be susceptible to significant change. Loans and leases deemed uncollectible are charged against the allowance, while recoveries are credited to the allowance. Management adjusts the level of the allowance through the provision for loan and lease losses, which is recorded as a current period expense. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> systematic methodology for assessing the appropriateness of the allowance includes: (1) general reserves reflecting historical loss rates by loan type, (2) specific reserves for risk-rated credits based on probable losses on an individual or portfolio basis and (3) qualitative reserves based upon current economic conditions and other risk factors.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The loan portfolio is stratified into loan classifications that have similar risk characteristics. The general allowance is based upon historical loss rates using a weighted three-year rolling average of the historical loss experienced within each loan classification.&nbsp;&nbsp;The qualitative factors used to adjust the historical loss experience address various risk characteristics of the Company&#x2019;s loan and lease portfolio include evaluating: (1) trends in delinquencies and other non-performing loans, (2) changes in the risk profile related to large loans in the portfolio, (3) changes in the growth trends of categories of loans comprising the loan and lease portfolio, (4) concentrations of loans and leases to specific industry segments, and (5) changes in economic conditions on both a local and national level, (6) quality of loan review and board oversight, (7) changes in lending policies and procedures, and (8) changes in lending staff.&nbsp;&nbsp;Each factor is assigned a value to reflect improving, stable or declining conditions based on management&#x2019;s best judgment using relevant information available at the time of the evaluation. Adjustments to the factors are supported through documentation of changes in conditions in a report accompanying the allowance calculation. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The specific reserves are determined utilizing standards required under ASC Topic 310.&nbsp;&nbsp;A loan is considered impaired when it is probable that interest and principal will not be collected according to the contractual terms of the loan agreement. Non-accrual loans and loans restructured under a TDR are evaluated for impairment on an individual basis considering all known relevant factors that may affect loan collectability such as the borrower&#x2019;s overall financial condition, resources and payment record, support available from financial guarantors and the sufficiency of current collateral values (current appraisals or rent rolls for income producing properties), and risks inherent in different kinds of lending (such as source of repayment, quality of borrower and concentration of credit quality). Non-accrual loans that experience insignificant payment shortfalls generally are not classified as impaired. Management determines the significance of payment delays and payment shortfalls on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration all of the circumstances surrounding the loan and the borrower, including the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, the borrower&#x2019;s prior payment record and the amount of the shortfall in relation to the principal and interest owed. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">43</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Impairment is measured on a loan by loan basis for commercial and industrial loans, commercial real estate loans and construction loans by either the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#x2019;s effective interest rate or the fair value of the collateral if the loan is collateral dependent.&nbsp;&nbsp;The estimated fair values of substantially all of the Company&#x2019;s impaired loans are measured based on the estimated fair value of the loan&#x2019;s collateral. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> obtain third-party appraisals to establish the fair value of real estate collateral.&nbsp;&nbsp;Appraised values are discounted to arrive at the estimated selling price of the collateral, which is considered to be the estimated fair value. The discounts also include estimated costs to sell the property. For commercial and industrial loans secured by non-real estate collateral, such as accounts receivable, inventory and equipment, estimated fair values are determined based on the borrower&#x2019;s financial statements, inventory reports, accounts receivable aging or equipment appraisals or invoices. Indications of value from these sources are generally discounted based on the age of the financial information or the quality of the assets. Large groups of smaller balance homogeneous loans are collectively evaluated for impairment. Once a loan is determined to be impaired it will be deducted from the portfolio balance and the net remaining balance will be used in the general and qualitative analysis. A specific reserve is established for an impaired loan for the amount that the carrying value exceeds its estimated fair value.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The amount of the allowance is reviewed and approved</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> by the CLO, CFO, CCO</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and the Chief Risk Officer (&#x201C;CRO&#x201D;) on at least a quarterly basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management believes that the allowance for loan and lease losses at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> is adequate. However, its determination requires significant judgment, and estimates of probable losses inherent in the credit portfolio can vary significantly from the amounts actually observed. While management uses available information to recognize probable losses, future changes to the allowance may be necessary.&nbsp;&nbsp;These changes could be based in the credits comprising the portfolio and changes in the financial condition of borrowers, as the result of changes in economic conditions.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, regulatory agencies, as an integral part of their examination process, periodically review the credit portfolio and the allowance. Such review may result in additional provisions based on their judgment of information available at the time of each examination.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">At</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, OREO assets acquired through the tax lien portfolio were comprised of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">60 </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">properties</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, were valued at $7</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.2 million</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and were primarily located in New Jersey</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">transferred $2.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">7</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million to OREO which represented </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">31</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> separate properties.&nbsp;&nbsp;During </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Company sold 4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">8</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> of the tax lien properties, received proceeds of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4.7</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million, and recorded net gains of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">859 thousand</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> as a result of these sales. Additionally, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> recorded impairment charges of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">578 thousand</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> in </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> related to the tax lien properties.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">During the third quarter of 2015, we reached an agreement with a tax payer, which was settled through a bankruptcy court. Under the agreement the tax payer is required to pay us monthly interest payments and annual principal reduction payments for the next three years. In exchange we transferred title to the property back to the tax payer while maintaining a lien on the property. After receiving a principal reduction payment of $250,000, we transferred the remaining balance of $995,000 to tax liens. No gain or loss was recorded on this transaction. At December 31, 2014, OREO assets acquired through the tax lien portfolio were $9.4 million and were </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">comprised of 79 properties.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The Company is working to satisfactorily sell the remaining OREO properties.&nbsp;&nbsp;However</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we recognize</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> that the successful disposition of the properties, specifically the land, will likely take considerable time.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Shareholders&#x2019; equity </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">attributable to the Company </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">grew</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;$</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">9.7</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million, or </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">15.6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%, from </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">62.2</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">71.9</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The increase was related to</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">net income of $11.0 million for 2015 which was partially offset by other comprehensive loss of</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$1.4 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;The other comprehensive loss was </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">mostly related to </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">a decline </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">in the valuation</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> of the investment portfolio</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The distributions </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">to non-controlling interests of $524 thousand and $266 thousand for 2015 and 2014, respectively, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">were to the 40% owners </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">of RBA Leasing and were for tax distribution</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">s.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Asset Liability Management</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The primary functions of asset-liability management are to ensure adequate liquidity and maintain an appro</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">priate balance between interest-earning assets and interest-</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">bearing liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;This process is overseen by the Asset-Liability Committee (&#x201C;ALCO&#x201D;) which monitors and controls, among other variables, the liquidity, balance sheet structure and interest rate risk of the consolidated company within policy parameters established and outlined in the ALCO Policy which are reviewed by the Board of Directors at least annually. Additionally,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> the ALCO committee meets month</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ly and reports on liquidity and</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> interest rate sensitivity and projects financial performance in various interest rate scenarios.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Liquidity:</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Liquidity is the ability to ensure that adequate funds will be available to meet </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> financial commitments as they become due. In managing its liquidity position, all sources of funds are evaluated, the largest of which is deposits. Also taken into consideration are securities maturing in one year or less, other short-term investments and the repayment of loans. These sources provide alternatives to meet </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> short-term liquidity needs. Longer liquidity needs may be met by issuing longer-term deposits and by raising additional capital. The liquidity ratios are specifically defined as the ratio of net cash, available FHLB and other lines of credit, and unpledged marketable securities relative to both total deposits and total liabilities.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> generally target liquidity ratios equal to or greater than 12% and 10% of total deposits and total liabilities</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, respectively. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, liquidity as</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a percent of deposits was 67</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">% and liquidity as a per</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">cent of total liabilities was 5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%.&nbsp;&nbsp;At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, liquidity</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> as a percent of deposits was </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">67</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">% and liquidity as a per</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">cent of total liabilities was 5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">3</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management believes that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> liquidity position continues to be adequate and meets or exceeds the liquidity target set forth in the Asset/Liability Management Policy.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management believes that due to its financial position, it will be able to raise deposits as needed to meet liquidity demands.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, any financial institution could have unmet liquidity demands at any time.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our funding decisions can be influenced by unplanned events, which include, but are not limited to, the inability to fund asset growth, difficulty renewing or replacing funds that mature, the ability to maintain or draw down lines of credit with other financial institutions, significant customer withdrawals of deposits, and market disruptions. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We have</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a liquidity contingency plan in the event liquidity falls below an acceptable level, however in today&#x2019;s economic environment, events could arise that may render sources of liquid funds unavailable in the future when required.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ALCO meets monthly to monitor liquidity management.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In connection with a prior bank regulatory examination, the FDIC concluded, based upon its interpretation of the Consolidated Reports of Condition and Income (the &#x201C;Call Report&#x201D;) instructions and under regulatory accounting principles (&#x201C;RAP&#x201D;), that income from Royal Bank&#x2019;s tax lien business should be recognized on a cash basis, not an accrual basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank&#x2019;s current accrual method is in accordance with U.S. GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank disagrees with the FDIC&#x2019;s conclusion and filed the</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> Call Report for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and the previous </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">21</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> quarters in accordance with U.S. GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;The change in the method of revenue recognition for the tax lien business for regulatory accounting purposes affects Royal Bank&#x2019;s capital ratios as shown below.&nbsp;&nbsp;The resolution of this matter will be decided by additional joint regulatory agency guidance which includes the Federal Reserve Bank, the FDIC, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (&#x201C;OCC&#x201D;).</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;">ITEM 7A.&nbsp;&nbsp;QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURE ABOUT MARKET RISK</font><a name="ITEM7AQUANTITATIVEANDQUALITATIVEDISCLOSU"></a>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">A</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">n interest rate</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> simulation model is used to estimate the impact of various changes, both upward and downward, in market interest rates and volumes of assets and liabilities on net interest income and net income.&nbsp;&nbsp;This model produces an interest rate exposure report that forecasts changes in the economic value of equity (&#x201C;EVE&#x201D;) and net interest income under alternative interest rate environments.&nbsp;&nbsp;This model assumes that the change in interest rates occurs immediately.&nbsp;&nbsp;The EVE is the difference between the present value of the expected future cash flows from Royal Bank&#x2019;s existing assets and the present value of the expected future cash flows from Royal Bank&#x2019;s existing liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;The assumptions used in evaluating the vulnerability of earnings and capital to changes in interest rates are based on management&#x2019;s considerations of past experience, current position and anticipated future economic conditions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The interest rate sensitivity of assets and liabilities as well as the estimated effect of changes in interest rates on the EVE and net interest income could vary substantially if different assumptions are used or actual experience differs from what the calculations may be based.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The simulation model indicates that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we are</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> outside of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our policy limits in the EVE </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">increasing rate scenarios for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">200, 300 and 400 basis points</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">but within policy limits </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">for rates up 100 basis points.&nbsp;&nbsp;We are within our policy limits for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">all changes in </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">net interest income</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> scenarios</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;The cause of the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">EVE </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">policy exceptions is primarily related to extension risk within the Company&#x2019;s investment portfolio</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">; the demand for fixed rate loans in this sustained low rate environment; the composition of deposits, and the lower capital from the prior period losses</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;In a rising interest rate environment general expectations are for</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> prepayments of principal to slow down which cause the life of the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">mortgage-backed and CMO securities to extend.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management continues to work on changing the mix of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">interest-earning assets to mitigate this risk.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In December 2015, the Federal Reserve Bank raised short-term interest rates 25 basis points.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We do not expect this singular event to have a significant impact on net interest income in 2016.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on the simulation results below we expect to remain within our policy limits.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The calculated estimates of changes in the EVE as of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and net interest income for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> for Royal Bank are as follows:</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:1pt;">&nbsp;</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 12pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Interest-Rate Sensitivity:</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;&nbsp;Interest rate sensitivity is a function of the re-pricing characteristics of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> assets and liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;These include the volume of assets and liabilities re-pricing, the timing of re-pricing, and the interest rate sensitivity gaps which are a continual challenge in a changing ra</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">te environment.&nbsp;&nbsp;In managing our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> interest rate sensitivity positions, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> seek to develop and implement strategies to control exposure of net interest income to risks associated with interest rate movements.&nbsp;&nbsp;The interest rate sensitivity report examines the positioning of the interest rate risk exposure in a changing interest rate environment.&nbsp;&nbsp;Ideally, the rate sensitive assets and liabilities will be maintained in a matched position to minimize interest rate risk.&nbsp;&nbsp;The interest rate sensitivity analysis is an important management tool; however, it does have some inherent shortcomings.&nbsp;&nbsp;It is a &#x201C;static&#x201D; analysis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although certain assets and liabilities may have similar maturities or re-pricing, they may react in different degrees to changes in market interest rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, re-pricing characteristics of certain</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> assets and liabilities may vary substantially within a given period.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 10pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The following table summarizes re-pricing intervals for interest earning assets and interest bearing liabilities as of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, and the difference or &#x201C;GAP&#x201D; between them on an actual and cumulative basis for the periods indicated. A gap is considered positive when the amount of interest rate sensitive assets exceeds the amount of interest rate sensitive liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;During a period of falling interest rates, a positive gap would tend to adversely affect net interest income, while a negative gap would tend to result in an increase in net interest income.&nbsp;&nbsp;During a period of rising interest rates, a positive gap would tend to result in an increase in net interest income while a negative gap w</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ould tend to affect net interest income adversely.&nbsp;&nbsp;At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we were</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> in a lia</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">bility sensitive position of $</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2.3</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million, which indicates that within one year the re-pricing of liabilities is sooner than the re-pricing of assets.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The method of analysis of interest rate sensitivity in the table above has a number of limitations.&nbsp;&nbsp;Certain assets and liabilities may react differently to changes in interest rates even though they re-price or mature in the same time periods.&nbsp;&nbsp;The interest rates on certain assets and liabilities may change at different times than changes in market interest rates, with some changes in advance of changes in market rates and some lagging behind changes in market rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;Also, certain assets have provisions, which limit changes in interest rates each time the interest rate changes and for the entire term of the loan.&nbsp;&nbsp;Prepayments and withdrawals experienced in the event of a change in interest rates may deviate significantly from those assumed in the interest rate sensitivity table.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, the ability of some borrowers to service their debt may decrease in the event of an interest rate increase.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">1.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Basis of Financial Statement Presentation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 13.55pt;text-indent: -13.55pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Nature of Operations</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Royal Bancshares of Pennsylvania, Inc. (</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x201C;Royal Bancshares&#x201D;, the &#x201C;Company&#x201D;, &#x201C;We&#x201D; or &#x201C;Our&#x201D;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">), through its wholly-owned subsidiary Royal Bank America (&#x201C;Royal Bank&#x201D;) offers a full range of banking services to individual and corporate customers primarily located in the Mid-Atlantic states.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank competes with other banking and financial institutions in certain markets, including financial institutions with resources substantially greater than its own.&nbsp;&nbsp;Commercial banks, savings banks, savings and loan associations, credit unions and brokerage firms actively compete for savings and time deposits and for various types of loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;Such institutions, as well as consumer finance and insurance companies, may be considered competitors of Royal Bank with respect to one or more of the services it renders.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt 13.55pt;text-indent: -13.55pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">T</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">he accompanying </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">audited consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Royal Bancshares of Pennsylvania,&nbsp;Inc. and its wholly-owned subsidiaries, Royal Investments of Delaware,&nbsp;Inc., including Royal Investments of Delaware,&nbsp;Inc.&#x2019;s wholly owned subsidiary, Royal Preferred, LLC,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and Royal Bank America, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">including Royal Bank&#x2019;s subsidiaries, Royal Real Estate of Pennsylvania,&nbsp;Inc., Royal Investments America, LLC, RBA Property LLC, Narberth Property Acquisition LLC, Rio Marina LLC, and Royal Tax Lien Services, LLC (&#x201C;RTL&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank also has an </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">80%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">60%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ownership interest in Crusader Servicing Corporation (&#x201C;CSC&#x201D;) and Royal Bank America Leasing, LP, respectively. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The two Delaware trusts, Royal Bancshares Capital Trust I and Royal Bancshares Capital Trust II are not consolidated per requirements under Financial Accounting Standards Board (&#x201C;FASB&#x201D;) Accounting Standards Codification (&#x201C;ASC&#x201D;) Topic 810, &#x201C;Consolidation&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 810&#x201D;).</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> These consolidated financial statements reflect the historical information of the Company. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> All significant intercompany transactions and balances have been eliminated in consolidation. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Use of Estimates</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In preparing the consolidated financial statements in accordance with United States generally accepted accounting principles (&#x201C;U.S. GAAP&#x201D;), management is required to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in the consolidated financial statements and the accompanying notes. These estimates and assumptions are based on information available as of the date of the consolidated financial statements; therefore, actual results could differ from those estimates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The principal estimates that are particularly susceptible to significant change in the near term relate to the allowance for loan and lease losses, the valuation of other real estate owned, the valuation of deferred tax assets, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">fair value measurements, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">other-than-temporary impairment losses on investment securities, net periodic pension costs and th</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">e pension benefit obligation.&nbsp;&nbsp;Descriptions of these estimates are in the following paragraphs.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">62</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>
