</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Significant Concentration of Credit Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Credit risk is one of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> most significant risks. It is critical for consistent profitability that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> effectively manage credit risk. Most of the Company&#x2019;s activities are with customers located within the Mid-Atlantic region of the country.&nbsp;&nbsp;&#x201C;Note 3 &#x2013; Investment Securities&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements discusses the types of securities in which the Company invests.&nbsp;&nbsp;&#x201C;Note 4 &#x2013; Loans and Leases&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements discusses the types of lending in which </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we engage</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We do</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> not have any portion of our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> business dependent on a single or limited number of customers, the loss of which would have </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">a material adverse effect on our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> business.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We have</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">93</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> investment portfolio in securities issued by government sponsored entities.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> tax certificate and other real estate owned portfolios have a geographic concentration in the State of New Jersey.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">No substantial portion of loans is concentrated within a single industry or group of related industries, except a significant majority of loans are secured by real estate.&nbsp;&nbsp;There are numerous risks associated with commercial and consumer lending that could impact the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay on a timely basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;They include, but are not limited to: the owner&#x2019;s business expertise, changes in local, national, and in some cases international economies, competit</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ion, government</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> regulation, and the general financial stability of the borrowing entity. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> commercial real estate, commercial and industrial and construction and land development loans comprised </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">7</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">0</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">%</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, respectively, of the loan portfolio.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We attempt</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to mitigate these risks through conservative underwriting policies and procedures which include an analysis of the borrower&#x2019;s business and industry history, its financial position, as well as that of the business owner.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> will also require the borrower to provide current financial information on the operation of the business periodically over the life of the loan.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, most commercial loans are secured by assets of the business or those of the business owner, which can be liquidated if the borrower defaults, along with the personal surety of the business owner.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">U.S. GAAP RAP Difference </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In connection with a prior bank regulatory examination, the Federal Deposit Insurance Company (&#x201C;FDIC&#x201D;) concluded, based upon its interpretation of the Consolidated Reports of Condition and Income (the &#x201C;Call Report&#x201D;) instructions and under regulatory accounting principles (&#x201C;RAP&#x201D;), that income from Royal Bank&#x2019;s tax lien business should be recognized on a cash basis, not an accrual basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank&#x2019;s current accrual method is in accordance with U.S. GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;Royal Bank disagrees with the FDIC&#x2019;s conclusion and filed the Call Report for </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and the previous </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">21</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> quarters in accordance with U.S. GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, the change in the manner of revenue recognition for the tax lien business for regulatory accounting purposes affects Royal Bank&#x2019;s and potentially </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> capital ratios as disclosed in &#x201C;Note 2 - Regulatory Matters and Significant Risks And Uncertainties&#x201D; and &#x201C;Note 16 - Regulatory Capital Requirements&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;The resolution of this matter will be decided by additional joint regulatory agency guidance which includes the Federal Reserve Bank, the FDIC, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (&#x201C;OCC&#x201D;).</font>
		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Investment Securities</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Management determines the appropriate classification of debt securities at the time of purchase and re-evaluates such designation as of each balance sheet date. Investments in debt securities that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we have</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> the positive intent and ability to hold to maturity are classified as held to maturity securities and reported at amortized cost.&nbsp;&nbsp;Debt and equity securities that are bought and held principally for the purpose of selling them in the near term are classified as trading securities and reported at fair value, with unrealized holding gains and losses included in earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Debt and equity securities not classified as trading securities, nor as held to maturity securities, are classified as available for sale securities and reported at fair value, with unrealized holding gains or losses, net of deferred income taxes (when applicable), reported in the accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) (&#x201C;AOCI&#x201D;) component of shareholders&#x2019; equity.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> did not hold trading securities nor had securities classified as held to maturity at December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Discounts and premiums are accreted/amortized to income by use of the level-yield method.&nbsp;&nbsp;Gain or loss on sales of securities available for sale is based on the specific identification method.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> evaluate declines in the fair value of securities for other-than-temporary impairment (&#x201C;OTTI&#x201D;) at least on a quarterly basis.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The term &#x201C;other-than-temporary&#x201D; is not intended to indicate that the decline is permanent, but indicates that the prospects for a near-term recovery of value is not necessarily favorable, or that there is a lack of evidence to support a realizable value equal to or greater than the carrying value of the investment.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> All investment securities are evaluated for OTTI under FASB ASC Topic 320, &#x201C;Investments-Debt &amp; Equity Securities&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 320&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;In determining whether OTTI exists, management considers numerous factors, including but not limited to: (1) the length of time and the extent to which the fair value is les</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">s than the amortized cost, (2) our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> intent to hold or sell the security, (3) the financial condition and results of the issuer including changes in capital, (4) the credit rating of the issuer, (5) analysts&#x2019; earnings estimate, (6) industry trends specific to the security, and (7) timing of debt maturity and status of debt payments.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Under ASC Topic 320, OTTI is considered to have occurred with respect to debt securities (1)&nbsp;if an entity intends to sell the security; (2)&nbsp;if it is more likely than not an entity will be required to sell the security before recovery of its amortized cost basis; or (3)&nbsp;the present value of the expected cash flows is not sufficient to recover the entire amortized cost basis.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Once a decline in value for a debt security is determined to be other-than-temporary, the other-than-temporary impairment is separated into (a) the amount of the total OTTI related to a decrease in cash flows expected to be collected from the debt security (the credit loss) and (b) the amount of the total OTTI related to all other factors. The amount of the total other-than-temporary impairment related to the credit loss is recognized in earnings. The amount of the total OTTI related to all other factors is recognized in other comprehensive income.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In determining </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> intent not to sell and whether it is more likely than not that </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> will be required to sell the investments before recovery of their amortized cost basis, management considers the following factors: current liquidity and</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> availability of other non-pledged assets that permits the investment to be held for an extended period of time but not necessarily until maturity, capital planning, and any specific asset liability committee goals or guidelines related to the disposition of specific investments. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Other Investment</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">This investment includes the Solomon Hess SBA Loan Fund, which </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> inve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">sted in to partially satisfy our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> community reinvestment requirement.&nbsp;&nbsp;Shares in this fund are not publicly traded and therefore have no readily determinable fair market value.&nbsp;&nbsp;An investor can have their investment in the Fund redeemed for the balance of their capital account at any quarter end with a </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">60</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">-day notice to the Fund.&nbsp;&nbsp;The investment in this Fund is recorded at cost.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Federal Home Loan Bank Stock</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">As a member of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Pittsburgh (&#x201C;FHLB&#x201D;), </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we are</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> required to purchase and hold stock in the FHLB to satisfy membership and borrowing requirements.&nbsp;&nbsp;The stock can only be sold to the FHLB or to another member institution, and all sales of FHLB stock must be at par. As a result of these restrictions, there is no active market for the FHLB stock. As of December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, FHLB stock totaled $2.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$2</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">6</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> million, respectively. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">FHLB stock is held as a long-term investment and its value is determined based on the ultimate recoverability of the par value. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> evaluate impairment quarterly. The decision of whether impairment exists is a matter of judgment that reflects management&#x2019;s view of the FHLB&#x2019;s long-term performance, which includes factors such as the following: (1) its operating </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">64</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">performance, (2) the severity and duration of declines in the fair value of its net assets related to its capital stock amount, (3) its liquidity position, and (4) the impact of legislative and regulatory changes on the FHLB.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on the capital adequacy and the liquidity position of the FHLB, management believes that the par value of its investment in FHLB stock will be realized.&nbsp;&nbsp;Accordingly, there is no impairment related to the carrying amount of the Company&#x2019;s FHLB stock as of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Loans Held for Sale</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and during the year ended </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015 and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2014</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> did not have any loans classified as loans held for sale (&#x201C;LHFS&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;Generally, loans are transferred from loans held for investment (&#x201C;LHFI&#x201D;) to LHFS at fair market value using expected net sales proceeds or collateral values when there is an intent to sell.&nbsp;&nbsp;Gains or losses on the sale of LHFS are recorded in non-interest income. Generally any subsequent credit losses on LHFS are recorded as a component of non-interest expense. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">During 2014, we received net proceeds of $3.8 million and recorded net gains of $232</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> thousand</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> as a result of loan sales.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Loans and Leases </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> originate commercial and real estate loans, including construction and land development loans primarily in the greater Philadelphia metropolitan area as well as selected locations throughout the mid-Atlantic region. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> also ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> participated with other financial institutions in selected construction and land development loans outside our geographic area. Loans and leases are classified as LHFI when management has the intent and ability to hold the loan or lease for the foreseeable future or until maturity or payoff.&nbsp;&nbsp;LHFI are stated at their outstanding unpaid principal balances, net of an allowance for loan and leases losses and any deferred fees or costs. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We utilize</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> the effective yield interest method for recognizing</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> interest income as required under FASB ASC Topic 310-20, &#x201C;Receivables&#x201D; - </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x201C;Nonrefundable Fees and Other Costs&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">310-</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">20&#x201D;)</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ASC </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">310-</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">20 also guides our accounting for nonrefundable fees and costs associated with lending activities such as discounts, premiums, and loan origination fees. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Interest income is accrued on the unpaid principal balance. Loan origination fees, net of certain direct origination costs, are deferred and recognized as an adjustment of the yield (interest income) of the related loans. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We are</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> generally amortizing these amounts over the contractual life of the loan.&nbsp;&nbsp;For loan modifications, a</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ny unamortized net fees or costs and any prepayment penalties from the original loan shall be recognized in interest income when the new loan is granted.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a concentration of credit risk in commercial real estate and construction and land development loans at December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> originate mainly small business, commercial real estate, middle market business and consumer loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, after thorough due diligence, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ha</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ve</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> purchased </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">specific commercial and commercial real estate loans and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">small residential loan pools. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">A substantial portion of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our borrowers</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x2019; ability to honor their contracts is dependent upon the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">regional economy including unemployment and the regional commercial and residential real estate markets</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The loans receivable portfolio is segmented into commercial loans, construction and development loans, residential loans, leases, tax certificates, and consumer loans. The commercial loan segment consists of the following classes: commercial real estate loans, multi-family real estate loans, and other commercial loans, which are also generally known as commercial and industrial loans or commercial business loans. The construction and development loan segment consists of the following classes: residential construction and commercial construction loans. Residential construction loans are made for the acquisition of and/or construction on a lot or lots on which a residential dwelling is to be built. Commercial construction loans are made for the purpose of acquiring, developing and/or constructing a commercial structure. The residential loan segment consists of the following classes: one- to four-family first lien residential mortgage loans, home equity lines of credit, and home equity loans.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We classify our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> leases as finance leases, in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 840, &#x201C;Leases&#x201D;. The difference between </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> gross investment in the lease and the cost or carrying amount of the leased property, if different, is recorded as unearned income, which is amortized to income over the lease term by the interest method.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificate segment&nbsp;&nbsp;includes </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">delinquent property tax certificates that have been acquired through public auctions in various jurisdictions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificates assume a lien position that is generally superior to any mortgage liens that are on the property and have certain foreclosure rights as defined by state law.&nbsp;&nbsp;The tax certificates are predominantly in New Jersey. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> ceased acquiring new tax certificates in 2010.&nbsp;&nbsp;Consumer loans includes cash secured and unsecured loans and </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">lines of credit. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">65</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Commercial Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> The commercial real estate loan portfolio consists primarily of loans secured by office buildings, retail and industrial use buildings, strip shopping centers, mixed-use and other properties used for commercial purposes primarily located in our market area. Although terms for commercial real estate and multi-family loans vary, the underwriting standards generally allow for terms up to 10 years with the interest rate being reset in the sixth year and with monthly amortization not greater than 25 years and loan-to-value ratios of not more than 80%. Interest rates are either fixed or adjustable and are predominantly based upon the prime rate or a borrowing rate from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Pittsburgh plus a margin. Prepayment fees are charged on most loans in the event of early repayment. Generally, the personal guarantees of the principals are obtained as additional collateral for commercial real estate and multi-family real estate loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Commercial and multi-family real estate loans generally present a higher level of risk than loans secured by one- to four-family residences. This greater risk is due to several factors, including the concentration of principal in a limited number of loans and borrowers, the effect of general economic conditions on income producing properties and the increased difficulty of evaluating and monitoring these types of loans. Furthermore, the repayment of loans secured by commercial and multi-family real estate is typically dependent upon the successful operation of the related real estate project. If the cash flow from the project is reduced (for example, if leases are not obtained or renewed, a bankruptcy court modifies a lease term, or a major tenant is unable to fulfill its lease obligations), the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay the loan may be impaired.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Our commercial business loans generally have been made to small to mid-sized businesses predominantly located in our market area. The commercial business loans are either a revolving line of credit or for a fixed term of generally 10 years or less. Interest rates are adjustable, indexed to a published prime rate of interest, or fixed. Generally, equipment, machinery, real property or other corporate assets secure such loans. Personal guarantees from the business principals are generally obtained as additional collateral. Generally, commercial business loans are characterized as having higher risks associated with them than single-family residential loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Our underwriting procedures include evaluations of the stability of the property&#x2019;s cash flow history, future operating projections, current and projected occupancy levels, location and physical condition. Generally, we require a debt service ratio (the ratio of net cash flows from operations before the payment of debt service to debt service) of not less than 120%. We also evaluate the credit and financial condition of the borrower, and if applicable, the guarantor. Appraisal reports prepared by independent appraisers are obtained on each loan to substantiate the property&#x2019;s market value, and are reviewed prior to the closing of the loan.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Construction and Development Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> We </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">originate construction loans to builders and developers predominantly in our market area. Construction and development loans are riskier than other loan types because they are more speculative in nature. Deteriorating economic or environmental conditions can negatively affect a project. Construction loans are also more difficult to evaluate and monitor.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to mitigate some of the risks inherent in construction lending, limits are placed on the number of units that can be built on a speculative basis based upon the reputation and financial position of the builder, his/her present obligations, the location of the property and prior sales in the development and the surrounding area. Additionally, the construction budget is reviewed prior to loan origination and the properties under construction are inspected. During the construction phase of a real estate project, the loan requires interest payments only.&nbsp;&nbsp;Construction loans generally are for 12 to 18 months with loan-to-value ratios of not more than 75%.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp;Most construction loans are assigned an initial risk rating of pass-watch due to the riskier nature of the loan.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Residential Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> Our residential mortgages were acquired in recent years in pool purchases and are secured primarily by properties located in our primary market and s</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">urrounding areas.&nbsp;&nbsp;We </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">originate home equity loans and home equity lines of credit in our market area with a </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">general </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">maximum amount of $250 thousand. The collateral must be the borrower&#x2019;s primary residence and the loan-to-value does not exceed 80%. Home equity lines of credit are variable rate and are indexed to the prime rate.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our home equity loans are either first or second liens and have a fixed rate.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">Consumer Loans:</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> We originate cash-secured and unsecured loans and lines of credit to individuals.&nbsp;&nbsp;Unsecured loans and lines of credit have a maximum amount of $15 thousand.&nbsp;&nbsp;Unsecured consumer loans generally have a higher interest rate than residential loans because they have additional credit risk associated with them.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">66</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">For all classes of loans receivable, with the exception of tax certificates, the accrual of interest is discontinued on a loan when management believes that the borrower&#x2019;s financial condition is such that collection of principal and interest is doubtful or when a loan becomes 90 days past due. When a loan is placed on non-accrual all unpaid interest is reversed from interest income. Interest payments received on impaired nonaccrual loans are normally applied against principal. Excess proceeds received over the principal amounts due on impaired non-accrual loans are recognized as income on a cash basis.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We recognize</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> income under the accrual basis when the principal payments on the loans become current and the collateral on the loan is sufficient to cover the outstanding obligation to the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;If these factors do not exist, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we do</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> not recognize income. Generally, loans are restored to accrual status when the loan is brought current, has performed in accordance with the contractual terms for a reasonable period of time (generally six months) and the ultimate collectibility of the total contractual principal and interest is no longer in doubt.&nbsp;&nbsp;The past due status of all classes of loans receivable is determined based on contractual due dates for loan payments.&nbsp;&nbsp;Tax certificates have no contractual maturity. Collection is dependent upon the tax payer&#x2019;s redemption of the lien, which includes principal interest and fees.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">A loan modification is deemed a troubled debt restructuring (&#x201C;TDR&#x201D;) when two conditions are met: 1) the borrower is experiencing financial difficulty and 2) a concession is made by </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">us</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> that would not otherwise be considered for a borrower with similar credit risk characteristics.&nbsp;&nbsp;All loans classified as TDRs are considered to be impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;TDRs are returned to an accrual status when the loan is brought current, has performed in accordance with the contractual restructured terms for a reasonable period of time (generally six months) and the ultimate collectibility of the total contractual restructured principal and interest is no longer in doubt.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> policy for TDRs is to recognize interest income on currently performing restructured loans under the accrual method.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> account for guarantees in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 460 &#x201C;Guarantees&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 460&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;ASC Topic 460 requires a guarantor entity, at the inception of a guarantee covered by the measurement provisions of the interpretation, to record a liability for the fair value of the obligation undertaken in issuing the guarantee.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">issue</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> financial and performance letters of credit.&nbsp;&nbsp;Financial letters of credit require </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">us</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to make a payment if the customer&#x2019;s condition deteriorates, as defined in agreements.&nbsp;&nbsp;Performance letters of credits require </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">us</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to make payments if the customer fails to perform certain non-financial contractual obligations.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 12pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> loan and lease portfolio (the &#x201C;credit portfolio&#x201D;) is subject to varying degrees of credit risk. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The allowance for loan and lease losses (the &#x201C;allowance&#x201D;) represents management&#x2019;s estimate of losses inherent in the loan and lease portfolio as of the statement of financial condition date and is recorded as a reduction to loans and leases. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The allowance is increased by the provision for loan and lease losses, and decreased by charge-offs, net of recoveries. Loans deemed to be uncollectible are charged against the allowance, and subsequent recoveries, if any, are credited to the allowance. All, or part, of the principal balance of loans receivable are charged off to the allowance as soon as it is determined that the repayment or collateral recovery of all, or part, of the principal balance is highly unlikely.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The allowance represents an estimation made pursuant to FASB ASC Topic 450, &#x201C;Contingencies&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 450&#x201D;) or FASB ASC Topic 310, &#x201C;Receivables&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 310&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;The adequacy of the allowance is determined through evaluation of the credit portfolio, and involves consideration of a number of factors, as outlined below, to establish a prudent level. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> consider that the determination of the allowance involves a higher degree of judg</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">ment and complexity than our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> other significant accounting policies. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> systematic methodology for assessing the appropriateness of the allowance includes: (1) general reserves reflecting historical loss rates by loan type, (2) specific reserves for risk-rated credits based on probable losses on an individual or portfolio basis and (3) qualitative reserves based upon current economic conditions and other risk factors.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> We also have a</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> reserve for unfunded lending commitments, which represents management&#x2019;s estimate of losses inherent in those commitments.&nbsp;&nbsp;The reserve for unfunded loan commitments is adjusted by a provision for credit losses on off-balance sheet credit exposures and is recorded in other liabilities on the consolidated statement of financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The loan portfolio is stratified into loan classifications that have similar risk characteristics. The general allowance is based upon historical loss rates using a </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">three</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">-year rolling average of the historical loss experienced within each loan segment.&nbsp;&nbsp;The qualitative factors used to adjust the historical loss experience address various risk characteristics of the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> loan and lease portfolio include evaluating: (1) trends in delinquencies and other non-performing loans, (2) changes in the risk profile related to large loans in the portfolio, (3) changes in the growth trends of categories of loans comprising the loan and lease portfolio, (4) concentrations of loans and leases to specific industry segments, (5) changes in economic conditions </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">67</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">on both a local and national level, (6) quality of loan review and board oversight, (7) changes in lending policies and procedures, and (8) changes in lending staff. Each factor is assigned a value to reflect improving, stable or declining conditions based on management&#x2019;s best judgment using relevant information available at the time of the evaluation. Adjustments to the factors are supported through documentation of changes in conditions in a report accompanying the allowance calculation. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The allowance calculation methodology includes further segregation of loan classes into risk rating categories. The borrower&#x2019;s overall financial condition, repayment sources, guarantors and value of collateral, if appropriate, are evaluated annually for commercial and construction and development loans or when credit deficiencies arise, such as delinquent loan payments, for all loans. Credit quality risk ratings include regulatory classifications of special mention, substandard, doubtful and loss. Loans classified as special mention have potential weaknesses that deserve management&#x2019;s close attention.&nbsp;&nbsp;If uncorrected, the potential weaknesses may result in deterioration of the repayment prospects.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans classified as substandard have a well-defined weakness or weaknesses that jeopardize the repayment of the debt.&nbsp;&nbsp;They include loans that are inadequately protected by the current sound net worth and paying capacity of the obligor or of the collateral pledged, if any.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans classified as doubtful have all the weaknesses inherent in loans classified substandard with the added characteristic that collection or liquidation in full, on the basis of current conditions and facts, is highly improbable.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans classified as a loss are considered uncollectible and are charged to the allowance.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans not classified as special mention, substandard, doubtful or loss are rated pass.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The specific reserves are determined utilizing standards required under ASC Topic 310.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We identify</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> a loan as impaired when it is probable that interest and principal will not be collected according to the contractual terms of the loan agreement.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Non-accrual loans and loans restructured under a TDR are evaluated for impairment on an individual basis considering all known relevant factors that may affect loan collectability such as the borrower&#x2019;s overall financial condition, resources and payment record, support available from financial guarantors and the sufficiency of current collateral values (current appraisals or rent rolls for income producing properties), and risks inherent in different kinds of lending (such as source of repayment, quality of borrower and concentration of credit quality). Management determines the significance of payment delays and payment shortfalls on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration all of the circumstances surrounding the loan and the borrower, including the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, the borrower&#x2019;s prior payment record and the amount of the shortfall in relation to the principal and interest owed. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Impairment is measured on a loan by loan basis for commercial and industrial loans, commercial real estate loans and construction loans by either the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#x2019;s effective interest rate or the fair value of the collateral if the loan is collateral dependent.&nbsp;&nbsp;The estimated fair values of substantially all of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> impaired loans are measured based on the estimated fair value of the loan&#x2019;s collateral. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> obtain third-party appraisals or real estate brokers&#x2019; opinions (&#x201C;BPOs&#x201D;) to establish the fair value of real estate collateral.&nbsp;&nbsp;Appraised values or BPOs are discounted to arrive at the estimated selling price of the collateral, which is considered to be the estimated fair value less estimated costs to sell the property. For commercial and industrial loans secured by non-real estate collateral, such as accounts receivable, inventory and equipment, estimated fair values are determined based on the borrower&#x2019;s financial statements, inventory reports, accounts receivable aging or equipment appraisals or invoices. Indications of value from these sources are generally discounted based on the age of the financial information or the quality of the assets. Large groups of smaller balance homogeneous loans are collectively evaluated for impairment. A specific reserve is established for an impaired loan for the amount that the carrying value exceeds its estimated fair value. Once a loan is determined to be impaired it will be deducted from the portfolio balance and the net remaining balance of the portfolio will be used in the general and qualitative analysis.</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Based on management&#x2019;s comprehensive analysis of the loan and lease portfolio, management believes the current level of the allowance is adequate at December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">. However, its determination requires significant judgment, and estimates of probable losses inherent in the credit portfolio can vary significantly from the amounts actually observed. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">While management uses the best information available to make allowance evaluations, adjustments to the allowance may be necessary based on changes in economic and other conditions or changes in accounting guidance. In addition, the FDIC, as an integral part of its examination processes, periodically reviews our allowance for loan and lease losses. The FDIC may require the recognition of adjustments to the allowance for loan and lease losses based on their judgment of information available to them at the time of their examinations. To the extent that actual outcomes differ from </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

In accordance with ASC Topic 715, &#x201D;Compensation &#x2013; Retirement Benefits&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 715&#x201D;), </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we recognize</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> the Plan&#x2019;s over-funded or under-funded status as an asset or liability with an offsetting adjustment to AOCI.&nbsp; ASC Topic 715 requires the determination of the fair value of a plan&#x2019;s assets at the company&#x2019;s year-end and the recognition of actuarial gains and losses, prior service costs or credits, transition assets or obligations as a component of AOCI.&nbsp; These amounts were previously netted against the plan&#x2019;s funded status in </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> consolidated Balance Sheet. The Plan does not have assets</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;We plan to fund a substantial portion of the pension plan obligations through existing Company owned life</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> insurance policies.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Stock Compensation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">FASB ASC Topic 718, &#x201C;Compensation-Stock Compensation&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 718&#x201D;) requires that the compensation cost relating to share-based payment transactions be recognized in consolidated financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;The costs are measured based on the fair value of the equity or liability instruments issued.&nbsp;&nbsp;ASC Topic 718 covers a wide range of share-based compensation arrangements including stock options, restricted share plans, performance-based awards, share appreciation rights, and employee share purchase plans.&nbsp;&nbsp;The effect of ASC Topic 718 is to require entities to measure the cost of employee services received in exchange for stock options based on the grant-date fair value of the award, and to recognize the cost over the period the employee is required to provide services for the award.&nbsp;&nbsp;ASC Topic 718 permits entities to use any option-pricing model that meets the fair value objective in the Statement.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> recorded compensation expense relating to stock options and restricted stock of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$78</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> thousand </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$17</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> thousand </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">during 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, respectively.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, the Company had a director stock-based plan, an employee stock-based plan, and a long-term incentive compensation plan, which are more fully described in &#x201C;Note 18 &#x2013; Stock Compensation Plans&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Trust Preferred Securities</font>

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Royal Bancshares Capital Trust I/II (&#x201C;Trusts&#x201D;) issued mandatory redeemable preferred stock to investors and loaned the proceeds to the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Trusts hold, as their sole asset, subordinated debentures issued by the Company in 2004.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We do</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> not consolidate the Trusts as ASC Topic 810 precludes consideration of the call option embedded in the preferred stock when determining if the Company has the right to a majority of the Trusts expected returns.&nbsp;&nbsp;The non-consolidation results in the investment in common stock of the Trusts to be included in other assets with a corresponding increase in outstanding debt of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">$774</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> thousand</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the income accrued on the Company&#x2019;s common stock investments is included in other income.&nbsp;&nbsp;Refer to &#x201C;Note 10 &#x2013; Borrowings and Subordinated Debentures&#x201D; to the Consolidated Financial Statements for more information.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Derivatives and Hedging</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In support of our</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> asset liability management process, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> will implement derivative hedging strategies with the intent of reducing interest rate risk and economic value of equity risk. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> account for derivatives in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 815 &#x201C;Derivatives and Hedging&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 815&#x201D;). </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> formally designate</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> derivatives a</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">s cash flow hedges and document</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> the strategy for entering into the transactions and the method of assessing ongoing effectiveness.&nbsp;&nbsp;Changes in the fair value of the derivative are recognized in other comprehensive income (loss) until the underlying forecasted transaction is recognized in earnings. The ineffective portion of a derivative&#x2019;s change in fair value is recognized in earnings immediately. To determine fair value, </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">we use</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> third party pricing models that incorporate assumptions about market conditions and risks that are current at the reporting date.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">We do</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> not use derivative instruments for speculative purposes.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Derivative instruments qualify for hedge accounting treatment only if they are designated as such on the date on which the derivative contracted is entered and are expected to be, and are, effective in substantially reducing interest rate risk arising from the assets and liabilities identified as exposing the Company to risk. Those derivative financial instruments that do not meet the hedging criteria discussed below would be classified as undesignated derivatives and would be recorded at fair value with changes in fair value recorded in income. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Derivative hedge contracts must meet specific effectiveness tests (i.e., over time the change in their fair values due to the designated hedge risk must be within </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">80</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">125</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> percent of the opposite change in the fair values of the hedged assets or liabilities). Changes in fair value of the derivative financial instruments must be effective at offsetting changes in the fair value of the hedged items due to the designated hedge risk during the term of the hedge. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We formally assess</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, both at the hedges&#x2019; inception, and on an on-going basis, whether derivatives used in hedging transactions have been highly effective in offsetting changes in cash flows of hedged items and whether those derivatives </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">70</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#toc"><font style="display:inline;color:#0563C1;font-size:10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">are expected to remain highly effective in subsequent periods. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> discontinue hedge accounting when (a) it determines that a derivative is no longer effective in offsetting changes in cash flows of a hedged item; (b) the derivative expires or is sold, terminated or exercised; (c) probability exists that the forecasted transaction will no longer occur; or (d) management determines that designating the derivative as a hedging instrument is no longer appropriate. In all cases in which hedge accounting is discontinued and a derivative remains outstanding, </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> will carry the derivative at fair value in the consolidated financial statements, recognizing changes in fair value in current period income in the consolidated statement of income. Cash flows resulting from the derivative financial instruments that are accounted for as hedges of assets and liabilities are classified in the cash flow statement in the same category as the cash flows of the items being hedged.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;text-decoration:underline;">Income Taxes</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> account for income taxes in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 740-10, &#x201C;Accounting for Uncertainty in Income Taxes&#x201D;,</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> (&#x201C;ASC 740</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> which includes guidance related to accounting for uncertainty in income taxes, which sets out a consistent framework to determine the appropriate level of tax reserves to maintain for uncertain tax positions. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> had </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">no</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> material unrecognized tax benefits or accrued interest and penalties as of December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We classify interest and penalties as an element of tax expense.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">The Company and its subsidiaries file a consolidated federal income tax return.&nbsp;&nbsp;Income taxes are allocated to the Company and its subsidiaries based on the contribution of their income or use of their loss in the consolidated return.&nbsp;&nbsp;Separate state income tax returns are filed by the Company and its subsidiaries. As of December 31, 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">5</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">, tax years 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> through 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> are subject to federal examination by the IRS and years 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">1</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> through 201</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">4</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> are subject to state examination by various state taxing authorities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Tax regulations are subject to interpretation of the related tax laws and regulations and require significant judgment to apply.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">Federal and state income taxes have been provided on the basis of reported income or loss.&nbsp;&nbsp;The amounts reflected on the tax returns differ from these provisions </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">principally </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">due to temporary differences in the reporting of certain items for financial reporting and income tax reporting purposes. The tax effect of these temporary differences is accounted for as deferred taxes applicable to future periods. Deferred income tax expense or benefit is determined by recognizing deferred tax assets (&#x201C;DTA&#x201D;) and liabilities (&#x201C;DTL&#x201D;) for the estimated future tax consequences attributable to differences between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and liabilities and their respective tax bases. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled.&nbsp;&nbsp;The effect on deferred assets and liabilities of a change in tax rates is recognized in earnings in the period that includes the enactment date.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We are required to establish a valuation allowance for DTAs and record a charge to income or shareholders' equity if management determines, based on available evidence at the time the determination is made, that it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized in future periods. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">In evaluating our ability to recover deferred tax assets, </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> consider all available positive and negative evidence, including past operating results </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">and projections of </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">future taxable income. In determining future taxable income, assumptions are made for the amount of taxable income, the reversal of temporary differences and </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">potentially </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">the implementation of feasible and prudent tax planning strategies. </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">This process involves significant management judgment about assumptions that are subject to change from period to period based on changes in tax laws or variances between projected operating performance, actual results and other factors. </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">While these estimates and judgments are inherently subjective, they are consistent with the plans and estimates management uses to manage </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">our</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> business.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;color:#000000;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">In the fourth quarter of </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">2015, we released a portion of our valuation allowance previously recorded on the net DTAs.&nbsp;&nbsp;In evaluating the need for a valuation allowance, we estimate future taxable income based on management approved business plans and potential tax planning strategies.&nbsp; </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">At </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2015</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">, the DTA valuation allowance was $3</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">0</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">6</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> million compared to </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">$39</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">1</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> million at </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">December 31, 2014</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">The ability to recogni</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">ze the remaining deferred tax assets that continue to be subject to a valuation allowance will be evaluated on a quarterly basis to determine if there are any significant events that would affect the ability to utilize these deferred tax assets.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> There can be no assurance, however, as to when </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">we</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> could be in a position to recapture </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">the remaining</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> DTA valuation allowance.</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> Refer to &#x201C;Note 1</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;">2</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;font-size:10pt;"> &#x2013; Income Taxes&#x201D;</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> to the Consolidated Financial Statements for more information.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman,Times,serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:10.2941176470588%;margin-right:10.2941176470588%;">

			<font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">We</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> report comprehensive income (loss) in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 220, &#x201C;Comprehensive Income&#x201D; (&#x201C;ASC Topic 220&#x201D;), which requires the reporting of all changes in equity during the reporting period except investments from and distributions to s</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">hareholders.&nbsp;&nbsp;Net income </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">is a component of comprehensive income (loss) with all other components referred to in the aggregate as other comprehensive income (loss).&nbsp;&nbsp;Comprehensive income (los</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">s) consists of net income</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> and other comprehensive income (loss).&nbsp;&nbsp;Other comprehensive income (loss) includes unrealized gains and losses on available for sale investment securities, non-credit related losses on other-than-temporarily impaired investment securities, adjustment to net periodic pension cost, and</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;"> adjustment to the </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">fair </font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">value of swap</font><font style="display:inline;font-size:10pt;">s.</font>
